meta.title: Who really said "A little knowledge is a dangerous thing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Alexander Pope wrote "A little LEARNING is a dangerous thing" in An Essay on Criticism (1711). The "knowledge" version is a famous later misquote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A little knowledge is a dangerous thing'?
meta.ogDescription: Pope's real line is "A little learning is a dang'rous thing" (1711). "Knowledge" is a well-worn paraphrase, not his wording.

answer.label: Not Pope’s words — a misquote of “A little learning…”
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Pope’s, but he wrote “A little learning is a dang’rous thing” in An Essay on Criticism (1711) — not “knowledge.” The “knowledge” wording is a later paraphrase that hardened into a catchphrase; it appears nowhere in Pope’s poem.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
A little Learning is a dang’rous Thing;
Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian Spring:
There shallow Draughts intoxicate the Brain,
And drinking largely sobers us again.
trail: Pope’s original couplet reads “A little learning is a dang’rous thing” in the Project Gutenberg text of An Essay on Criticism — the word is learning, not knowledge.

Quote Investigator traces how the “knowledge” variant grew out of Pope’s line, quoting Thomas Henry Huxley (1877): “The saying that a little knowledge is a dangerous thing is, to my mind, a very dangerous adage.”
By Huxley’s day the “knowledge” catchphrase was already common enough to argue against — evidence the swap is a genuine, long-standing paraphrase of Pope, not his own phrasing.
source.excerptNote: Part II of An Essay on Criticism. Pope’s word is “learning” — superficial study — not “knowledge.”

author.name: Alexander Pope
author.heading: About Alexander Pope
author.bio: Alexander Pope was the leading poet of early-18th-century England, famous for his polished heroic couplets and biting satire (The Rape of the Lock, The Dunciad). He published An Essay on Criticism anonymously in 1711, at just 23; its epigrams — “To err is human, to forgive divine,” “fools rush in where angels fear to tread” — are among the most-quoted lines in English.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most common misquotations in English — the wording people cite is not quite what Pope wrote.

items.why: Pope wrote “A little learning is a dang’rous thing” in An Essay on Criticism (1711). The popular “a little knowledge is a dangerous thing” substitutes a word he never used in that line.
The “knowledge” form spread as a proverb through the 1800s; by 1877 Thomas Henry Huxley was already pushing back on it, per Quote Investigator. No single author owns the reworded version.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Pope’s and the couplet is real — but the accurate quotation is “A little learning is a dang’rous thing,” per the original text.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Pope’s point is subtle: a little learning is worse than none because it breeds false confidence. The next lines make the metaphor — shallow sips from the Pierian spring (sacred to the Muses) “intoxicate the brain,” while drinking deeply sobers you again.

The swap to “knowledge” flattens that meaning. Learning is the process of study; knowledge is the result — which is exactly why Huxley objected that some knowledge, however small, is better than none.
